manuscript_title: Optimal stimulation sites are not the most affected:

required_revisions.text: [R1-02] Still open and blocking. Run a hypergeometric or permutation test on the Fig. 6C overlap (121 sites; sets of 35 and 33; observed 11 shared against ~9.5 expected), report the exact p-value in the figure caption, the Results text and Methods, and revise the wording to whatever the test supports. If the overlap is not significantly below chance, 'largely disjoint' must be removed from the caption, the Results and the title framing. This is the single most important outstanding item because it is the premise of the title.

[R1-01] Still open and blocking, and the revision moved against it. Re-anchor the abstract and the corresponding Results paragraph to the leakage-free estimate: report the ~78% population-average LOPO net cure as the primary generalizable result, and label the ~100% per-patient 121-way argmax figure explicitly as an upper bound obtained under per-patient site selection on the fitted cohort. Move Fig. S9 into the main Results flow. Also report the 17.5%->42.5% baseline misclassification shift in Results, not only in Methods and the Supplement. The current abstract rewrite does the reverse of this and must be revised again.

[R1-04] Still open and blocking. Qualify the causal/biological language at the point of first claim, not only in the Discussion on p.18. Specifically: add an explicit 'within the fitted model' clause to the abstract sentences asserting that the required correction is 'intrinsically distributed' and that optimal targets are 'cortical and heterogeneous'; state immediately before Fig. 4 that the reservoir is fit to infraslow BOLD connectivity rather than electrophysiology, so an 'intervention' here is an abstract input to regional FC dynamics; and state that f_eig derives from the spectrum of J, not from patient data.

[R1-05] Still open and blocking. Provide (a) the random seed(s) used to generate J and J_in, or a statement that results are averaged over seeds — the methods audit records this as a hard reproduction blocker, since the paper specifies one fixed reservoir but not how to regenerate it; (b) pinned versions for Python, NumPy, scikit-learn, nilearn and Matplotlib, ideally as a deposited environment file; and (c) a participant demographics table (age, sex, MMSE or equivalent, disease stage) for the 40/40 and 145/41 cohorts, plus the QC/exclusion criteria actually applied. Table S1 currently gives session and subject counts only.

[R1-03] Still open and blocking, but narrowed. Either add the hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (re-running the DeltaW pathology ranking and LDA-resonant site selection across a small grid of N and spectral radius, reporting whether the cortical/subcortical dissociation survives), OR state plainly in the Limitations that robustness to reservoir architecture is untested and include the authors' own argument — that a single shared reservoir is used across subjects and both selection criteria, so architecture dependence cannot by itself produce the divergence — as an explicitly labelled argument rather than a demonstration. Either route closes this item; the current draft does neither.

[R1-10] Still open. In the 'In-silico stimulation' Results subsection, add the short paragraph distinguishing read-out interpolation (alpha) from input oscillation amplitude (A), and 2–3 plain-language sentences at first mention distinguishing the transductive SVD embedding from leave-one-patient-out reconstruction, making explicit which forms of leakage each analysis is and is not exposed to.

[R1-06] Still open. Report bootstrapped 95% CIs alongside mean+/-SD for the AUROC and balanced-accuracy metrics in Fig. 3, state in Methods that the +/-0.12 on the tangent-space SVM is the SD of the 25 fold-level AUROCs from the nested 5x5 CV, and add the supplementary table of fold values. For Fig. S1, state explicitly that the N=100–200 projections are unvalidated extrapolations.

[R1-07] Still open. Add the numerical definition of 'physiological amplitude' to Methods (the proposed RMS_pert/RMS_base <= 2 is adequate) and reference that threshold at each use of 'physiological' or 'supra-physiological' in Results, so that the claim that focal targeting fails 'at any amplitude' becomes checkable.

[R1-09 / methodology-5] Still open. Either re-run the tangent-space SVM benchmark on the matched 40 CC + 40 AD cohort with the same fold structure as the main classifiers and report that value alongside the larger-cohort number, or withdraw the 'lower end of the benchmark' comparison. As written, the preprocessing (GSR, 557+145 sessions) and CV differ from the main analysis and the comparison is not interpretable as stated.

[R1-08] Narrowed and still open. Cite a standard Riemannian/tangent-space FC methods reference (e.g. Barachant et al.) in the Methods description of the tangent-space SVM benchmark. The request to cite Luppi et al. (2026) and Bonni et al. (2026) is withdrawn: the reviewer could not verify those works exist, and the authors are right to decline to cite unverified references.

minor_suggestions: Deposit a frozen, versioned snapshot of the analysis repository (Zenodo/OSF DOI) and add a README table mapping each script to the figures and tables it produces. The authors have agreed to this; doing it in the next round rather than 'at time of publication' would let a reviewer verify it.

Fix the abstract's characterisation of 97.5% vs 100% as 'comparable' — the authors' own proposed phrasing ('reaches 97.5% reclassification at lower dose, nearly matching the 100% open-loop rate') is fine and matches the main text on p.12.
Add the AI-use disclosure statement the authors offered, to Acknowledgments or Methods.

Provide DOIs for Fox et al. (2014), Koch et al. (precuneus rTMS) and Vogel et al. (2020), and confirm the Koch venue/year — the citation audit found a 2025 Alzheimer's Research & Therapy paper that may be the intended reference. Non-blocking, but cheap to resolve.
The citation audit flagged Jaeger (2001, GMD Report 148) and Martorell et al. (2019, Cell) as unverifiable through its tools. Neither is load-bearing; a DOI or handle for each would close the record.

Consider stating explicitly, where the AUROC comparison is made, that the model's justification is perturbability rather than diagnostic gain. The Discussion already makes this argument well and it answers a reviewer objection directly; surfacing it earlier would prevent the same reading recurring.
Note in Methods whether any multiple-comparison correction was applied across the Mann–Whitney comparisons reported in Figs. 1C and 4A, or state that none was and that the p-values are descriptive.

weaknesses.text: {HARD} The two intervention protocols—read-out interpolation (α parameter, Figs. 4–5) and oscillatory stimulation (amplitude A, Figs. 5–7)—are introduced without clear upfront distinction. The text states 'α is distinct from the oscillation amplitude A below' (Methods, p. 22) but this appears only after results are presented. A reader encountering Fig. 4 does not immediately know whether the perturbation is a theoretical read-out edit or a physical drive. Suggest: clarify in the main-text Results section before Fig. 4 that two protocols are being compared and what each represents. (only partly addressed in the revision: The abstract now states 'a single-site drive at the node whose connectivity is most altered fails to revert the classification even at supra-physiological amplitudes, whereas selecting each patient's site by its effect on the disease discriminant achieves complete, individualised reclassification from one site' (p. 1), which distinguishes the two approaches. However, the main Results section still does not explicitly introduce the two protocols before Fig. 4. The text jumps from 'Shifting an AD read-out toward the CC template over all regions ("full-W") moved both classifiers' scores into the CC range' (p. 8) directly to Fig. 4 without first stating that two distinct intervention families—read-out interpolation and oscillatory stimulation—will be compared. The phrase 'α is distinct from the oscillation amplitude A below' appears only in Methods (p. 22), after all main results are presented. A reader encountering Fig. 4 still cannot immediately tell whether the perturbation is theoretical or physical without reading the figure caption carefully. The distinction is now clearer in the abstract but remains inadequately signposted in the Results narrative before the figures.)

{HARD} The transductive vs. leave-one-out cross-validation distinction is critical to the leakage-free claim but is relegated to Methods (p. 23, 'Leakage-free target selection') and Fig. S9. The main text (p. 12) states 'Honest cross-validation does raise the baseline...' without first explaining what 'honest' means or why the transductive embedding used throughout Figs. 3–5 is not honest. A reader unfamiliar with transductive learning may not grasp why Fig. S9 is necessary or what it changes. Suggest: briefly define transductive vs. leave-one-out in Results before presenting the main stimulation findings, or move the leakage-free analysis to the main text. (only partly addressed in the revision: The main text now states 'To isolate what makes a single-site intervention work, we contrasted the two ways of acting on one node (Fig. 5): the theoretical read-out correction, which interpolates that node's read-out column toward the control mean, and the physical resonant drive' (p. 11), which explicitly names the two protocols. However, the transductive vs. leave-one-out distinction remains inadequately explained in the main text. The passage 'To test the therapy-target reclassification for classifier leakage we repeated the FC-lag analysis under leave-one-AD-patient-out cross-validation' (p. 12) assumes the reader already understands what 'leakage' means and why the transductive embedding (used in Figs. 3–5) is leaky. The text does not define 'transductive' or explain why the SVD embedding and LDA discriminant fit on all patients constitutes leakage. A reader unfamiliar with transductive learning will not grasp why Fig. S9 is necessary or what it changes about the main claims. The leakage-free analysis is now in the main text (p. 12) rather than Methods, but the conceptual distinction is still not explained.)

{HARD} The term 'physiological amplitude' is used repeatedly (Figs. 4C, 5, Methods p. 22) but is never formally defined in the main text. The Methods state 'supra-physiological amplitude limits' and reference 'fig. S10' for 'physiological diagnostics', but S10 defines it only as 'RMSpert/RMSbase > 1'. What is the threshold for 'physiological'? Is it RMSpert/RMSbase ≤ 2, ≤ 1, or something else? This ambiguity undermines the claim that focal strategies fail 'at any amplitude' (p. 9). Suggest: define the physiological amplitude threshold explicitly in Results or Methods. (still unaddressed in the revision: The term 'physiological amplitude' is still not formally defined in the main text. The abstract and Results repeatedly use phrases like 'supra-physiological amplitudes' (p. 9, 'even at supra-physiological amplitudes, shifting only a minority of patients') and 'physiological amplitude limits' (p. 9, 'failed to revert the classification within physiological amplitude limits'). The Methods state 'supra-physiological values, i.e. beyond the RMS of the endogenous teacher-forcing drive' (p. 23) and reference 'fig. S10' for 'physiological diagnostics'. Fig. S10 shows RMSpert/RMSbase but does not state a threshold; the caption says 'distributed correction stays near the endogenous amplitude, focal correction does not' but does not define 'near'. The main text never states whether 'physiological' means RMSpert/RMSbase ≤ 1, ≤ 2, or some other threshold. This ambiguity undermines the claim that focal strategies fail 'at any amplitude' because the reader cannot determine what amplitude range was tested as 'physiological'.)

{SOFT} The term 'read-out' is used in three distinct senses: (1) the linear decoder W, (2) the output y = W⊤x, and (3) the feature space derived from W (G-space). While context usually disambiguates, the first mention of 'read-out geometry' (p. 5) could be clearer. Suggest: use 'read-out weights' for W, 'read-out output' for y, and 'read-out geometry' for the feature space, or define each sense at first use. (only partly addressed in the revision: The manuscript now uses 'read-out weights' for W in some places (e.g., 'the geometry of the read-out weights across patients', p. 5) and 'read-out' more loosely elsewhere. However, the three senses are still not consistently distinguished. The term 'read-out' appears in the abstract as 'Two complementary read-outs of the fitted models' (p. 1), which refers to feature spaces (G-space and FC-lag), not W itself. In Methods, 'read-out' is used for both W and y = W⊤x without explicit distinction. The phrase 'read-out geometry' (p. 5) is now slightly clearer in context but is not formally defined at first use. The inconsistency is reduced but not resolved; a glossary or explicit definitions at first use would fully resolve this.)

{SOFT} Figure 2I caption states 'median ± IQR' but the plot shows error bars that appear symmetric; IQR is typically asymmetric around the median. Are these actually SD or SEM? The caption should match the plot. Suggest: clarify whether the bands represent IQR or SD/SEM. (still unaddressed in the revision: Figure 2I caption still states 'median ± IQR, all sessions' but the plot shows symmetric error bars. IQR is typically asymmetric around the median. The caption has not been corrected to clarify whether the bands represent IQR, SD, or SEM. This is a minor but unresolved ambiguity in the figure.)

{SOFT} The phrase 'a distributed change in the model's connectivity kernel' (abstract, p. 1) is never formally defined. What is the 'connectivity kernel'? Is it the read-out W, the recurrent weights J, or something else? The term appears again in Results (p. 9) but without definition. Suggest: define 'connectivity kernel' at first use or replace with a more standard term. (only partly addressed in the revision: The abstract now avoids the term 'connectivity kernel' entirely, replacing 'a distributed change in the model's connectivity kernel' with 'a coordinated, multi-site change of the model connectivity' (p. 1). However, the Results section still uses the term without definition: 'The quantity ∥ΔW∥ is best understood not as a localiser of pathology but as an estimate of the change in the model's spatiotemporal connectivity kernel required to map a patient's dynamics onto the control template' (p. 8). The term 'connectivity kernel' is never formally defined; a reader must infer from context that it refers to the read-out weights W or the effective input-to-output transfer function. The abstract improvement is partial; the main text still contains the undefined term.)

[clarity-9] still unaddressed in the revision: The question about the formal definition of 'physiological amplitude' and whether the threshold is RMSpert/RMSbase ≤ 2 has not been answered. The Methods state 'supra-physiological values, i.e. beyond the RMS of the endogenous teacher-forcing drive' (p. 23) but do not define the boundary between physiological and supra-physiological. Fig. S10A shows that full-W correction stays within ~2× baseline amplitude, but the text does not state whether this is the intended threshold for 'physiological'. This remains unresolved.

The abstract's claim that the optimal sites are 'cortical and heterogeneous' (p. 1) is not fully supported by the evidence presented. Fig. 6D shows the therapy sites are 'predominantly cortical' but also include subcortical structures (hippocampus, brainstem, thalamus, caudate, putamen). The abstract's statement is accurate but could be clearer about the subcortical minority. (not raised in the previous round)

The abstract states 'a real-time closed-loop controller reaches comparable efficacy at lower dose using only causally available information' (p. 1), but the main text (Fig. 5D–F) shows the closed-loop controller achieves 97.5% reclassification (39/40) versus 100% for open-loop (40/40), which is not 'comparable' in the strict sense—it is slightly lower. The abstract's phrasing is misleading. (introduced by the revision)

questions: What is the formal threshold for 'physiological amplitude'? Is it RMSpert/RMSbase ≤ 1, ≤ 2, or some other value? The Methods mention 'beyond the RMS of the endogenous teacher-forcing drive' but do not state a numerical boundary.

In the transductive embedding (Figs. 3–5), the SVD basis and LDA discriminant are fit on all patients, then classifiers are evaluated on held-out folds. Why is this not considered leakage? A brief explanation in the main text (e.g., 'the embedding is transductive, meaning the basis is fit on all patients but the classifier is trained and tested on disjoint folds') would clarify why Fig. S9 is necessary.
Figure 2I caption states 'median ± IQR' but the error bars appear symmetric. Should this be 'median ± SD' or 'median ± SEM'?

The abstract claims the closed-loop controller reaches 'comparable efficacy' to open-loop, but Fig. 5D–F shows 97.5% vs. 100%. Should the abstract state '97.5%, nearly matching the 100% open-loop rate' (as the main text does on p. 12) rather than 'comparable'?

In Results (p. 8), the term 'connectivity kernel' is used without definition. Does this refer to the read-out weights W, the recurrent weights J, or the effective input-to-output transfer function? A formal definition would strengthen the mechanistic claim.

weaknesses.text: No confidence intervals reported on the primary classification metrics (AUROC, balanced accuracy) across folds; only mean±SD is given. A 95% CI on AUROC for each classifier would strengthen claims about the modest but above-chance performance and its comparison to the tangent-space benchmark. (still unaddressed in the revision: The manuscript still reports AUROC and balanced accuracy as mean±SD over folds (e.g., Fig. 3A–D: 'mean over folds; bands, ±1SD'). No 95% confidence intervals are provided on the primary classification metrics. The text states 'mean±SD' but does not give the actual CI bounds, which would quantify uncertainty on the modest ~0.70 AUROC claims more precisely than a band width.)

The tangent-space SVM benchmark (AUROC 0.75±0.12) is reported as mean±SD over nested CV, but the definition of 'SD' is ambiguous—is this the SD of fold-level AUROCs, or a pooled estimate? The out-of-fold ROC (Fig. 3E) shows AUC≈0.71, which sits at the lower end of the reported range, raising a question about how the mean and SD are computed. (still unaddressed in the revision: The tangent-space SVM benchmark is still reported as 'AUROC 0.75±0.12 (out-of-fold 0.71; Fig. 3E)' in the Results section. The Methods clarify that this is 'mean±SD over a nested 5×5 patient-level CV,' but it remains ambiguous whether the ±0.12 is the SD of the 25 fold-level AUROCs or a pooled estimate. The discrepancy between the reported mean (0.75) and the out-of-fold ROC (0.71) is not explained. A clearer statement of how the SD was computed (e.g., 'SD of 25 fold-level AUROCs') would resolve this.)

In Fig. 3A–D, the 'reference noise σ' and 'reference K' are chosen by 'marginal-mean AUROC across classifiers,' but it is unclear whether this selection was made on the training set only or involved the test set in any way. If the reference slices were chosen post-hoc to maximise performance, this could introduce a soft bias. (only partly addressed in the revision: The Methods section now states: 'Reference slices were chosen by the marginal-mean AUROC across classifiers and the complementary axis.' However, it does not explicitly state whether this selection was made on the training set only or involved the test set. The text says 'The SVD embeddings were built transductively (across all patients) while the classifiers were trained and tested on disjoint folds,' which clarifies that the embedding is transductive but does not clarify whether the K and σ selection involved test-set inspection. A statement such as 'K and σ were selected on the training set only' or 'K and σ were chosen post-hoc from the full cross-validation grid' would fully resolve this.)

The learning-curve extrapolation (Fig. S1) fits a saturating power law m(N) = A − B·N^(−C) to leave-one-patient-out data, but no confidence band or uncertainty quantification is provided for the projected AUROC at N=100 and N=200. The 68% band shown is from the fit covariance, but the extrapolation range is large and the fit quality is not reported (R², residual plot). (only partly addressed in the revision: Fig. S1 now includes a 'saturating power-law fit' with a '68% band from the fit covariance' and projects AUROC≈0.76 at N=100 and ≈0.80 at N=200. However, no R² or residual plot is provided to assess fit quality, and the extrapolation range is large (from N=40 to N=200). The caption states 'saturating power law m(N) = A − B·N^(−C) is fitted to each metric' but does not report the fitted parameters (A, B, C) or their uncertainties, limiting reproducibility and sensitivity analysis.)

Effect sizes (e.g., the dissociation between pathology sites and therapy sites) are reported qualitatively (e.g., 'only 11 sites shared, ~31% and ~33% of each set'; Fig. 6C) but not with a formal overlap metric or Jaccard index, making the magnitude of the dissociation harder to quantify. (still unaddressed in the revision: Fig. 6C reports 'of the 35 distinct pathology sites (top-5 union across patients) and 33 distinct per-patient therapy sites (personalised LDA-resonant targets) identified across the 40 AD patients share only 11 sites, the great majority of each set is exclusive to its own criterion.' This is stated qualitatively as ~31% and ~33% overlap. No formal overlap metric (Jaccard index, Sørensen–Dice, or other) is provided to quantify the dissociation magnitude or allow comparison to other datasets.)

The per-patient amplitude×frequency stimulation landscape (Fig. S8) shows individual and population-level heatmaps, but no summary statistic (e.g., median or IQR of the amplitude needed to cross the decision boundary at resonance) is provided across the 40 patients, limiting reproducibility and generalisability assessment. (still unaddressed in the revision: Fig. S8 shows per-patient (A, B) and population-level (C, D) amplitude×frequency heatmaps, but no summary statistic (median, IQR, or range) is provided for the amplitude needed to cross the decision boundary at resonance across the 40 patients. The caption describes the landscape but does not report, e.g., 'median amplitude at f_eig = X ± Y (IQR),' limiting reproducibility and generalisability assessment.)

In the oscillatory stimulation analysis (Methods, 'Oscillatory stimulation'), the choice of frequency sweep range [0, 0.5] cycles/step is not justified, and it is unclear whether this range was chosen a priori or post-hoc based on preliminary results. (still unaddressed in the revision: The Methods section ('Oscillatory stimulation') states 'Frequencies were swept over f ∈ [0, 0.5] cycles/step' but does not justify this range or state whether it was chosen a priori or post-hoc. The text notes that f_eig ≈ 0.077 cycles/step is the dominant eigenmode, which falls well within [0, 0.5], but does not explain why the upper bound of 0.5 was selected or whether a wider range was tested. A statement such as 'the range [0, 0.5] was chosen a priori to cover the infraslow and low-frequency bands' or 'a sensitivity analysis over [0, 1.0] yielded consistent results' would resolve this.)

The 'net cure' metric in Fig. S9 (fraction of AD-side patients moved to CC side by stimulation) is a sensible leakage-free measure, but the baseline misclassification rate (42.5% under LOPO) is substantially higher than the transductive baseline (17.5%), making the comparison between transductive and LOPO results harder to interpret without a clearer statement of what is being held constant. (only partly addressed in the revision: Fig. S9 now reports 'net cure' as 'the fraction of patients on the AD side at baseline that stimulation moves to the CC side' under both transductive and LOPO schemes. The caption states 'Honest cross-validation raises the baseline misclassification of AD as CC from 17.5% (transductive) to 42.5% (LOPO), so that only 23 of 40 AD patients lie on the AD side of the boundary unstimulated.' This clarifies the difference in operating points, but a side-by-side table comparing absolute reclassification rates (not just net cure) under both schemes would make the comparison more transparent and easier to interpret.)

No multiple-comparison correction is applied across the 121 sites tested in the per-site stimulation analysis (Fig. S6A, where 'almost every site is therapeutic on average'). Although the authors note that 120/121 sites move the score toward CC, no Bonferroni or FDR correction is mentioned, and it is unclear whether this is a single exploratory analysis or a hypothesis test. (still unaddressed in the revision: Fig. S6A reports 'almost every site is therapeutic on average at f_1 (A=4)' and states '120/121 sites move the score toward CC; only site 81 net-harmful.' The caption notes 'a safety argument for personalised targeting' but does not apply a multiple-comparison correction (Bonferroni, FDR) to determine which sites are significantly therapeutic versus which are indistinguishable from noise. The analysis is exploratory, but the claim '120/121 sites are therapeutic' should be qualified as 'move the mean score toward CC' without implying statistical significance, or a correction should be applied.)

[data_analysis-10] still unaddressed in the revision: The Methods section ('Leakage-free target selection') states that the personalised per-patient LDA-resonant site is 'an upper bound on achievable personalisation' but does not quantify this bound. Fig. S9B shows that the personalised LOPO target reaches ~100% net cure, whereas the population-average LOPO target reaches ~78%. However, the text does not state how much of the 100% is due to the per-patient argmax over 121 sites versus how much would be achieved by a fixed global site, or provide a sensitivity analysis (e.g., top-3, top-5 sites per patient) to quantify the cost of personalisation.

[data_analysis-11] still unaddressed in the revision: The Methods section ('In-silico stimulation') states 'α > 1 is over-correction' and notes 'the exact α=1 replacement can be insufficient: the reconstruction is closed-loop, so the reservoir state driven by the AD input keeps the FC partly AD-like even under the CC read-out, and crossing the decision boundary can require pushing past W_CC.' However, no sensitivity analysis is provided showing the effect of capping α at 1.0 or demonstrating that α=1 is empirically insufficient. A figure showing reclassification rate vs α with and without the α>1 range would clarify whether the over-correction is necessary or merely convenient.

[data_analysis-12] still unaddressed in the revision: The Methods section ('Read-out fitting') states that the read-out W is obtained by 'ridge-like regularised least squares with additive Gaussian noise of scale σ in the regressor,' with σ=0.025 as the default. However, the justification for this choice is not provided, and it is unclear whether σ was selected a priori or tuned to maximise performance. The text sweeps σ in Fig. 3C–D but does not state whether the sweep was performed on the training set only or involved the test set.

In the Methods section ('Classification'), the text states 'Performance was estimated by repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation (80/20 train/test, 10 repeats),' but it is unclear whether the 10 repeats use different random splits or the same splits with different random seeds. If the splits are the same across repeats, the reported SD may be artificially inflated or deflated. Clarification of the repeat structure would strengthen the reproducibility claim. (not raised in the previous round)

The learning-curve extrapolation (Fig. S1) uses leave-one-patient-out CV to estimate AUROC at different cohort sizes, but the text does not state whether the same held-out patient is used across all cohort sizes, or whether a fresh LOPO is performed for each N. This affects the interpretation of the learning curve and the validity of the extrapolation. (not raised in the previous round)

questions: Can you provide 95% confidence intervals (not just ±1 SD bands) on the primary AUROC and balanced-accuracy metrics in Fig. 3A–D? This would quantify uncertainty more precisely and allow readers to assess whether the modest ~0.70 AUROC is consistent with the tangent-space benchmark (0.75±0.12).

For the tangent-space SVM benchmark (AUROC 0.75±0.12), please clarify: is the ±0.12 the standard deviation of the 25 fold-level AUROCs, or a pooled estimate? How does the reported mean (0.75) relate to the out-of-fold ROC (0.71 in Fig. 3E)? A table showing the 25 fold-level AUROCs would resolve this.

In Fig. 3A–D, were the reference K and σ selected on the training set only, or did the selection involve inspection of test-set performance? If the latter, this could introduce selection bias. Please state explicitly: 'K and σ were chosen by marginal-mean AUROC on the training set only' or provide a sensitivity analysis showing that the results are robust to different K and σ choices.

For Fig. S1, please report the fitted parameters (A, B, C) of the power-law model m(N) = A − B·N^(−C), the R² of the fit, and a residual plot. Also, perform a sensitivity analysis: how do the projected AUROC values at N=100 and N=200 change if you fit a different saturating model (e.g., exponential, logistic)?

In Fig. 6C, please quantify the dissociation between pathology and therapy sites using a formal overlap metric (e.g., Jaccard index = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|). This would allow comparison to other datasets and make the magnitude of the dissociation more concrete.

In Fig. S8, please report summary statistics (median, IQR, range) for the amplitude A needed to cross the decision boundary at resonance f_eig across the 40 patients. This would strengthen the reproducibility and generalisability claims.

For the oscillatory stimulation analysis, please justify the frequency sweep range [0, 0.5] cycles/step: was it chosen a priori, or based on preliminary inspection? If the latter, please perform a sensitivity analysis over a wider range (e.g., [0, 1.0]) to confirm that f_eig is the true optimum.

In Fig. S9, please provide a side-by-side table comparing absolute reclassification rates (not just net cure) under transductive and LOPO schemes, to make the comparison more transparent. For example: 'Transductive: X% of 40 AD patients reclassified; LOPO: Y% of 23 AD-side patients reclassified.'

In Fig. S6A, the claim that '120/121 sites are therapeutic on average' should be qualified: are these sites significantly therapeutic (after multiple-comparison correction), or do they simply move the mean score toward CC? If the latter, please apply a Bonferroni or FDR correction to determine which sites are significantly different from zero effect.

In the Methods ('Leakage-free target selection'), you state that the personalised per-patient LDA-resonant site is 'an upper bound on achievable personalisation.' Can you quantify this bound? For example, what is the net cure rate if you restrict each patient to their top-3 or top-5 sites, rather than the top-1? This would show how much personalisation is necessary.

For the read-out interpolation (Figs. 4, S10), please provide a sensitivity analysis showing reclassification rate vs α with α capped at 1.0. Does capping α at 1.0 substantially reduce efficacy, or is the α>1 range merely a convenience? This would clarify whether over-correction is necessary or empirical.

weaknesses.text: SOFT: The manuscript does not acknowledge the use of any AI tools or large language models in analysis, manuscript preparation, or figure generation. Given the computational nature and the date (2026), a statement on AI use (if any) would strengthen transparency, even if none was used. (still unaddressed in the revision: The manuscript contains no disclosure of AI tool use in analysis, figure generation, or manuscript preparation. The Methods section describes computational pipelines (Python, NumPy, scikit-learn, nilearn, Matplotlib) but does not state whether any large language models, generative AI, or AI-assisted tools were used in any phase of the work. Given the computational nature of the work and the 2026 date, a statement on AI use (even if none was used) would strengthen transparency. The authors were asked to provide this disclosure but have not done so in the revision.)

[ethics-3] still unaddressed in the revision: The Data and code availability section states: 'ADNI data are available to qualified researchers upon registration and acceptance of the ADNI Data Use Agreement; in accordance with that agreement, the raw and derived imaging data are not redistributed here. All analysis and figure-generation code is openly available at github.com/cristianocapone/AD-reservoir-FC-stimulation.' This addresses the DUA restriction correctly, but the manuscript does not explicitly confirm that the GitHub repository contains only code and non-data outputs, not derived imaging data. weaknesses.text: HARD: The classifier is trained and tested on the same cohort (transductive embedding, Methods p. 21), and the therapy-target selection criterion is defined by its effect on that same discriminant. This creates a closed loop: the sites that 'cure' the patient are those that move the patient's score toward the CC distribution as defined by the training set. The leave-one-AD-patient-out cross-validation (Fig. S9) rebuilds the discriminant per fold, but the therapy-target selection still uses a per-patient argmax over 121 sites, each scored against the train-only threshold. This is not a fully independent validation—the personalised targets are still selected post-hoc to maximize effect on the discriminant, which is a form of overfitting to the classification objective. The manuscript acknowledges this as an 'upper bound' (Methods, p. 23), but the distinction between the personalised and population-average targets in Fig. S9 is not clearly explained in the main text, leaving ambiguity about which result is the honest one. (only partly addressed in the revision: The authors added Fig. S9 and explicitly discuss the distinction between transductive and leave-one-AD-patient-out (LOPO) cross-validation. They now state: 'the personalised figure still reflects a per-patient argmax over the 121 candidate sites and should be read as an upper bound on achievable personalisation, whereas the population-average result, a single global site selected on the training patients alone, is the conservative, fully out-of-sample estimate' (Methods, p. 23). This clarification is helpful and appears in the main text (Discussion, p. 15: 'personalised, model-informed targeting is required'). However, the main-text claims still emphasize the 100% personalised result (Abstract, p. 1; Fig. 5A) without consistently flagging it as an upper bound. The honest, fully independent estimate is the population-average LOPO result (~78% net cure, Fig. S9B), which is substantially weaker than the 100% personalised claim. The manuscript now acknowledges the distinction but does not fully integrate it into the narrative arc—readers may still take the 100% figure as the primary result.)

HARD: The model is fit to each subject's own data (Methods, Eq. 2), and the perturbation analysis (Figs. 4–5) modifies the read-out W or its input, then re-scores the same model on the same data (teacher-forced FC-lag features). This is not a true out-of-sample validation of the therapy effect. The closed-loop free-run (Fig. 5) is a step toward independence, but it still uses the same fitted model and the same subject's data. There is no held-out test set or independent cohort to verify that the therapy sites identified in one patient generalize to another, or that the dissociation between pathology and therapy sites is not an artifact of the model's fitting procedure. (still unaddressed in the revision: The authors added closed-loop free-run validation (Fig. 2I, Fig. 5) and LOPO cross-validation (Fig. S9), which are steps toward independence. However, the core issue remains: the therapy-target selection (LDA-resonant site) is still defined by its effect on the FC-lag discriminant, which is derived from the same cohort's data. The LOPO scheme rebuilds the discriminant per fold, but each held-out patient's personalised target is selected as the argmax of that patient's per-site effect on the train-only discriminant (Methods, p. 23). This is not a true out-of-sample validation of generalizability—it is a per-patient optimization against a train-only threshold, which is a form of post-hoc fitting. The manuscript does not test whether the therapy sites identified in one patient generalize to another patient, or whether the dissociation between pathology and therapy sites holds in an independent cohort. The closed-loop free-run (Fig. 5) uses the same fitted model and same subject's data, so it does not address the generalizability concern.)

HARD: The 'stimulation' is an abstract modification of the read-out W or its input, not a literal physical protocol. The mapping between in-silico amplitude (α or A) and a deliverable dose is 'approximate' (Discussion, p. 18), and the optimal frequency (f_eig ≈ 0.026 Hz) is derived from the BOLD-based model, not from electrophysiology or any independent measure of brain dynamics. The claim that 'the model prescribes where and how to stimulate' (Abstract, p. 1; Discussion, p. 17) overstates the translational validity of the prescription. The model is phenomenological and fit to infraslow BOLD correlations; it does not capture cellular mechanisms, neuromodulatory systems, or the actual biophysics of stimulation. The authors acknowledge this ('the reservoir is fit to infraslow BOLD connectivity, not electrophysiology', Discussion, p. 18), but the framing in the abstract and introduction suggests a more direct path to intervention than the evidence supports. (only partly addressed in the revision: The authors added a caveat in the Discussion (p. 18): 'these are model-level prescriptions: the reservoir is fit to infraslow BOLD connectivity, not electrophysiology, so an "intervention" here is an abstract input to the regional FC dynamics, and its optimal spatial pattern and (infraslow) frequency should be read as targets at the level of regional drive, not as cellular or oscillatory mechanisms. With that caveat, the focal, slowly-modulated character maps in spirit onto closed-loop, biomarker-guided neuromodulation; translating it to any specific technology, and validating it against electrophysiological or longitudinal outcomes, is left to future work.' This is a more honest framing than the abstract and introduction suggest. However, the abstract still claims 'the site to stimulate is not where connectivity is most altered but where the network is most therapeutically responsive' and 'optimal targets are cortical and heterogeneous', which could mislead readers into thinking the model provides a direct prescription for a physical intervention. The Discussion caveat is appropriate but buried; the abstract and introduction should be more cautious about translational claims.)

weaknesses.text: **HARD: Title and abstract claim causality without sufficient warrant.** The title states 'a distributed functional-connectivity signature of Alzheimer's disease' and the abstract claims 'the ideal correction that maps a patient's dynamics onto the control template is a distributed change'—but this is an observation about what the fitted model requires, not a causal discovery about the disease itself. The model is fit to cross-sectional data; it does not establish that the disease *is* distributed in the biological sense, only that the model's read-out deviations are distributed. The claim 'whether its FC signature reduces to a few focal sites has not been tested causally' (Introduction) frames the question as causal, but the answer—that the model requires distributed correction—does not settle whether the underlying disease pathology is focal or distributed; it only shows the model's representational geometry. This is a SOFT-to-HARD boundary: the framing invites a causal/biological reading that the evidence does not support. (only partly addressed in the revision: The abstract now states more carefully that 'the required correction is intrinsically distributed: a coordinated, multi-site change of the model connectivity that no single-node edit reproduces.' This is more precise about what the model shows. However, the title remains 'Optimal stimulation sites are not the most affected' and the abstract still frames this as answering a causal question ('whether its signature reduces to a few focal sites has not been tested causally'). The paper does establish that the model's read-out requires distributed correction, but the framing still invites a reading that this settles whether the disease *is* distributed biologically. The Discussion (p. 15) does acknowledge 'Whether this dissociation reflects the biology of AD or the representational geometry of the model is a question our framework raises but cannot, on its own, settle', but this caveat is not in the abstract or title. The claim remains: the abstract should explicitly state that 'distributed' refers to the model's representational requirement, not a validated property of the disease itself.)

**HARD: Generalization beyond the fitted model.** The abstract and Results claim 'the site to stimulate is not where the read-out deviation is largest but where the network is most therapeutically responsive' as a general principle. However, this is demonstrated only within the fitted reservoir model on this cohort. Whether this dissociation holds in actual brain tissue, in other models, or in other cohorts is not tested. The claim is presented as a finding about neuromodulation strategy in general ('Optimal targets are cortical and heterogeneous: effective neuromodulation requires model-informed, personalised targeting'), but it is a finding about this model on this data. The Discussion does hedge ('Whether this dissociation reflects the biology of AD or the representational geometry of the model is a question our framework raises but cannot, on its own, settle'), but the abstract and main narrative do not, creating a scope mismatch. (only partly addressed in the revision: The abstract now adds 'personalised models' and emphasizes that targets are 'patient-specific', which is more careful. However, the abstract still states 'Optimal targets are cortical and heterogeneous: the site to stimulate is not where connectivity is most altered but where the network is most therapeutically responsive' without qualification that this is demonstrated only in the fitted model on this cohort. The Discussion (p. 15-16) does hedge appropriately: 'Whether this dissociation reflects the biology of AD or the representational geometry of the model is a question our framework raises but cannot, on its own, settle.' But the abstract and main narrative still present this as a general principle of neuromodulation strategy without stating the scope limitation upfront. The claim 'Optimal targets are cortical and heterogeneous' should be qualified as 'In this model, optimal targets are...' or moved to Discussion.)

**HARD: Causal language for in-silico perturbations.** The paper uses 'stimulation', 'intervention', 'drive', and 'cure' throughout to describe read-out interpolations and input oscillations applied to a phenomenological model. These are not stimulations in the neurobiological sense; they are mathematical modifications of a fitted linear read-out or inputs to a fixed random reservoir. The closed-loop section (Fig. 5) calls the controller 'adaptive (closed-loop) neuromodulation' and states 'a causally available, minimal-dose perturbation', but causality here is causal availability in the model's information flow, not causal efficacy in the brain. The Discussion acknowledges 'the reservoir is fit to infraslow BOLD connectivity, not electrophysiology, so an "intervention" here is an abstract input to the regional FC dynamics', but the main text and abstract do not carry this caveat, and the language ('reclassified', 'cured', 'therapeutic') implies a real intervention. This is HARD because the causal framing is misleading without the caveat front and center. (only partly addressed in the revision: The Discussion (p. 17) now includes a more prominent caveat: 'We emphasise, however, that these are model-level prescriptions: the reservoir is fit to infraslow BOLD connectivity, not electrophysiology, so an "intervention" here is an abstract input to the regional FC dynamics, and its optimal spatial pattern and (infraslow) frequency should be read as targets at the level of regional drive, not as cellular or oscillatory mechanisms.' This is helpful. However, the abstract and main text (e.g., 'reclassified', 'cured', 'therapeutic target', 'closed-loop controller') still use causal/clinical language without the caveat front and center. The abstract states 'achieving complete, individualised reclassification from one site' without noting this is in silico at supra-physiological amplitude. The Methods section (p. 22) clarifies 'In-silico stimulation: the model was used as a counterfactual testbed', but this is not in the abstract. The caveat in the Discussion is necessary but insufficient; the abstract should state explicitly that these are in-silico perturbations of a phenomenological model, not validated neuromodulation protocols.)

**SOFT: Claim about 'complete reclassification' under-hedged.** The abstract states 'selecting each patient's site by its effect on the disease discriminant achieves complete, individualised reclassification from one site'. Figure 5A shows 100% reclassification in the open-loop case, but this is achieved at supra-physiological amplitude (A=6, Fig. S10), and the closed-loop version reaches only 97.5% (39/40, Fig. 5D). The leakage-free version (Fig. S9) reaches ~100% for personalised targets but ~78% for the population-average site. The word 'complete' is accurate for the open-loop transductive case but not for the honest cross-validation, and the amplitude caveat is not in the abstract. (only partly addressed in the revision: The abstract now states 'achieving complete, individualised reclassification from one site, and a real-time closed-loop controller reaches comparable efficacy at lower dose using only causally available information.' This is more careful: it acknowledges the closed-loop version reaches 'comparable' (not complete) efficacy. Figure 5D shows 97.5% (39/40) for the closed-loop case. However, the abstract still uses 'complete' for the open-loop case without noting the supra-physiological amplitude (A=6, Fig. S10B showing ~44× baseline). The leakage-free result (Fig. S9) shows ~78% net cure for the population-average site and ~100% for personalised targets, but the abstract does not distinguish transductive from honest cross-validation. The claim 'complete, individualised reclassification' is accurate only for the transductive, open-loop, personalised case at supra-physiological amplitude. The abstract should either qualify 'complete' with the amplitude caveat or report the honest cross-validation result (~78–100% depending on personalisation level).)

**SOFT: 'Distributed' vs 'not focal' conflation.** The paper argues that because targeting the top-1 or top-5 most-deviant sites fails, the signature is 'distributed'. However, 'distributed' could mean (i) the pathology is spread across many regions, (ii) the discriminative signal requires many regions to read out, or (iii) the therapeutic effect requires many regions to achieve. The evidence shows (ii) and (iii) within the model, but does not distinguish whether the underlying pathology is truly distributed or whether the model's representational geometry simply requires a distributed read-out to capture a focal lesion. The Discussion hints at this ('Whether this dissociation reflects the biology of AD or the representational geometry of the model'), but the main claims treat 'distributed' as a property of the disease, not the model. (still unaddressed in the revision: The paper still conflates 'distributed' (a property of the disease) with 'not focal' (a property of the model's representational geometry). The abstract states 'the required correction is intrinsically distributed: a coordinated, multi-site change of the model connectivity that no single-node edit reproduces.' This is accurate about the model. However, the Discussion (p. 15) proposes a mechanistic interpretation: 'A plausible mechanistic account is that pathology originating in limbic hubs propagates along structural and functional connections, distributing its imprint on connectivity across the network; the discriminative signal then resides in the network-wide pattern, so that correcting the seed regions alone is insufficient.' This is speculative and not tested. The paper does not distinguish whether the distributed correction requirement reflects (i) distributed pathology, (ii) the model's inability to capture focal pathology in a distributed read-out, or (iii) the nonlinear relationship between read-out changes and FC changes. The claim 'the disease signature is not reducible to those focal nodes' (p. 8) is not established; what is established is that the model's read-out is not reducible to those nodes. The paper should state clearly: 'Within the fitted model, the discriminative signal requires distributed correction, but this does not establish whether the underlying pathology is focal or distributed.')

**SOFT: Learning-curve extrapolation (Fig. S1) presented without uncertainty bounds on the projection.** The paper extrapolates AUROC to N=100 and N=200 patients per group, projecting ~0.76 and ~0.80 respectively. These are point estimates from a power-law fit; the 68% band shown is the fit uncertainty, not a confidence interval on the extrapolation. The claim 'the modest present accuracy reflects sample size rather than a ceiling of the representation' is reasonable but depends on the extrapolation being accurate, which is not guaranteed. This is SOFT because the caveat is present but the projection is given prominent placement in the main narrative. (still unaddressed in the revision: Figure S1 still shows the extrapolation to N=100 and N=200 with a 68% band labeled as fit uncertainty, not a confidence interval on the extrapolation. The caption states 'saturating power law fit; shaded region = extrapolation beyond current cohort' and projects AUROC ≈0.76 at N=100 and ≈0.80 at N=200. The main text (p. 7) states 'an empirical extrapolation projects ∼0.76 AUROC at N=100 and ∼0.80 at N=200 patients per group, indicating that the modest accuracy reflects sample size rather than a ceiling of the representation.' This is presented as evidence that the modest accuracy is not a ceiling. However, the extrapolation assumes the power-law model holds beyond the observed range and that the fit uncertainty band is appropriate for projection. No bootstrap or cross-validation of the extrapolation is provided. The claim should be qualified: 'If the observed power-law trend continues, extrapolation projects...' or the extrapolation should be moved to supplementary with a caveat about its uncertainty.)

**SOFT: Anatomical interpretation of ΔW sites under-hedged.** The paper states 'The siteswiththelargestper-patientcorrectionmagnitude∥ΔW∥wereconsistentlysubcorticalandlimbic,mostfrequentlythe bilateral pallidum and nucleus accumbens, the brainstem and the amygdala', then notes 'these are, however, also among the most weakly inter-connected nodes of the parcellation, where a shared reservoir basis constrains the per-subject read-out least; the ranking should thus be read as indicating where the correction kernel carries its largest weights, not as an independently validated map of Alzheimer pathology.' This caveat is appropriate but buried in the text; the anatomical claim is stated first and prominently (Fig. 6A,B), creating an impression of validated pathology localization that the caveat undermines. (only partly addressed in the revision: The paper now states (p. 8): 'The siteswiththelargestper-patientcorrectionmagnitude∥ΔW∥wereconsistentlysubcorticalandlimbic,mostfrequentlythe bilateral pallidum and nucleus accumbens, the brainstem and the amygdala (Fig. 6A,B). These are, however, also among the most weakly inter-connected nodes of the parcellation, where a shared reservoir basis constrains the per-subject read-out least; the ranking should thus be read as indicating where the correction kernel carries its largest weights, not as an independently validated map of Alzheimer pathology.' This caveat is now in the main text, not buried. However, the anatomical claim is still stated first and prominently in Fig. 6A,B, and the Discussion (p. 16) states 'The regions whose read-out departed most from the control template were predominantly subcortical and limbic, bilateral pallidum and nucleus accumbens, brainstem and amygdala, structures of the limbic and basal-ganglia circuitry; several of these overlap with regions harbouring early neurofibrillary pathology in Braak staging, although they are also the most weakly inter-connected nodes of the parcellation, where the per-subject read-out is least constrained, so this correspondence should be treated as provisional rather than as a validated disease localiser.' The caveat is present but the anatomical interpretation is still given prominence. This is improved but still SOFT: the anatomical claim should be qualified in the figure caption or moved after the caveat.)

**HARD: Claim that 'pathology sites and therapeutic sites are largely disjoint' (Fig. 6 title) is not tested statistically.** The paper shows 11 of 35 pathology sites and 11 of 33 therapy sites overlap (~31% each), and states 'the great majority of each set is exclusive to that criterion'. However, no statistical test of whether this overlap is less than expected by chance is provided. If the 121 sites were randomly partitioned into two sets of 35 and 33, what overlap would be expected? Without this, the claim of dissociation is qualitative. This is HARD because the headline claim (Fig. 6 title, Discussion) rests on a quantitative comparison that is not formally tested. (still unaddressed in the revision: The paper still does not provide a statistical test of whether the overlap between pathology sites (35 distinct, top-5 union) and therapy sites (33 distinct, top-1 per patient) is less than expected by chance. Figure 6C shows 11 shared sites (~31% of each set) and states 'the great majority of each set is exclusive to that criterion.' However, no permutation test, hypergeometric test, or random-partition baseline is provided. If 121 sites were randomly partitioned into two sets of 35 and 33, the expected overlap would be ~9.5 sites by chance (35×33/121 ≈ 9.5). The observed 11 is only slightly higher. The claim 'pathology sites and therapeutic-stimulation sites are largely disjoint' (Fig. 6 title) is qualitative without a formal test. The paper should either (i) provide a permutation test showing the overlap is significantly less than expected by chance, or (ii) qualify the claim as 'show limited overlap' rather than 'largely disjoint.')

[rigor-9] still unaddressed in the revision: The paper does not address whether the resonant frequency f_eig ≈ 0.077 cycles/step is subject-specific or a fixed property of the reservoir's shared dynamics. The Methods (p. 22) states 'Because J (and hence its eigenspectrum) is fixed and shared across subjects, the resonance f_eig is a property of the model, not a subject-specific fit.' This clarifies that the resonance is not fit to the data, but it does not test whether the frequency tuning (Fig. S7A) is driven by the model's intrinsic resonance or by disease-specific FC-lag signal. The Discussion (p. 17) states 'The driving frequency that most efficiently moved a target toward the control distribution coincided with the model's intrinsic resonance', but does not test whether a different model with different eigenspectrum would yield a different optimal frequency. This is a limitation that should be acknowledged: the frequency prescription is derived from the model's fixed dynamics, not from the disease data, so it may not generalize to other models or to real neuromodulation.

[rigor-10] still unaddressed in the revision: The paper does not test whether the two read-outs (G-space and FC-lag) are capturing the same underlying signal or independent sources of weak discrimination. Figure 3 shows both reach comparable AUROC (~0.66–0.70) and plateau near K≈25, but no correlation or overlap analysis is provided. The caption (p. 7) states 'That two geometrically distinct read-outs reach a similar ceiling is itself consistent with a modest, distributed disease signal rather than a sharply localised one', but this is an interpretation, not a test. The paper should either (i) show that the two feature spaces are correlated and capture the same signal, or (ii) acknowledge that they may be independent weak classifiers that happen to plateau at similar accuracy, which would not support the claim of a distributed signal.

[rigor-11] still unaddressed in the revision: The paper uses a transductive embedding (SVD across all patients) for classification in Figs. 3–5, then applies leave-one-patient-out cross-validation. The Methods (p. 21) states 'The SVD embeddings were built transductively (across all patients) while the classifiers were trained and tested on disjoint folds.' This introduces leakage: the embedding is built on all patients, including the test set. The honest cross-validation (Fig. S9) rebuilds the embedding, discriminant, and threshold from training patients only. Figure S9 shows the leakage-free result (~78% net cure for population-average site, ~100% for personalised targets) differs from the transductive result (Figs. 3–5). The main results (Figs. 3–5) should either use the honest cross-validation or explicitly state that the transductive embedding introduces leakage and that Fig. S9 provides the honest estimate. Currently, the transductive result is presented as the primary finding, and the honest cross-validation is supplementary.

[rigor-12] still unaddressed in the revision: The paper does not provide a formal test of whether the observed dissociation between pathology sites (ΔW-ranked) and therapy sites (LDA-resonant) is statistically significant. The Discussion (p. 15) states 'the dissociation between the two site sets (Fig. 6) is therefore expected rather than paradoxical: a distributed kernel correction and a focal resonant drive are different interventions, and there is no reason their leading sites should coincide.' This is a post-hoc explanation, not a test. The paper should either (i) provide a permutation test showing the dissociation is significant, or (ii) acknowledge that the dissociation could arise by chance given the different selection criteria and the modest sample size (40 patients, 121 sites).

[rigor-13] still unaddressed in the revision: The abstract claims 'a real-time closed-loop controller reaches comparable efficacy at lower dose using only causally available information.' However, 'causally available' here means information available in the model's information flow (the model's own past output), not causal efficacy in the brain. The Methods (p. 22) clarifies 'an online controller reclassifies 39/40 (97.5%) of AD patients, nearly matching the 100% reached by a fixed open-loop drive, while cutting the mean stimulation amplitude by ∼44%', but the abstract does not note that this is still at supra-physiological amplitude (A=3.3, Fig. 5D) and that the 44% reduction is relative to the open-loop amplitude (A=6), not to baseline. The claim 'lower dose' is accurate relative to open-loop but misleading without the baseline context. The abstract should state 'lower dose than open-loop' or provide the absolute amplitude.
